drivers: Recurrent Horn of Africa droughts (2017, 2019, 2021-2023) decimated pastoralist livestock herds, the main livelihood and food source
Acute malnutrition classified IPC Phase 4 (Critical) per the July 2023 SMART survey; GAM well above emergency thresholds
High poverty rates, limited crop farming, and reliance on food aid in a vast arid county with sparse health infrastructure
Poor WASH access and recurrent disease outbreaks (cholera, measles) that worsen acute malnutrition
Garissa.testimony: Representative composite: Amina, a mother of four in Garissa Town, lost nearly all her goats during the 2022-2023 drought. Her two-year-old son was admitted to the IMAM outpatient therapeutic feeding program at Medina Health Centre with severe acute malnutrition; with Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food he recovered over six weeks, but the family remains food-insecure as rains continue to fail.
initiatives: Integrated Management of Acute Malnutrition (IMAM) program at sites like Medina Health Centre, supported by UNICEF
Save the Children IMAM and drought-response nutrition programs across Garissa sub-counties
National Drought Management Authority (NDMA) early warning and contingency response
Garissa.success_story: Garissa County expanded IMAM/CMAM outpatient therapeutic feeding across drought-affected sub-counties during the 2021-2023 Horn of Africa drought, with UNICEF and Save the Children supporting admission of thousands of children; an AI-based malnutrition early-warning tool co-developed with the Jameel Observatory is now being integrated to anticipate drought-driven spikes.

drivers: Over 60% of residents live in informal settlements (Kibera, Mathare, Mukuru) where stunting ranges 26-50% — far above the national average
Deep urban poverty and food insecurity: a KEMRI/CDC survey found ~90% of Kibera households had reduced dietary diversity
Poor WASH and overcrowding drive repeated infections (diarrhoea, respiratory) that compound chronic undernutrition
Low maternal education and sub-optimal infant and young child feeding (IYCF) practices in slum settings
Nairobi.testimony: Representative composite: Wanjiru, a single mother of three in Mathare, earns ~KSh 300 a day washing clothes. Rising food prices pushed her to skip meals so her children could eat; her youngest, 18 months, was diagnosed with moderate acute malnutrition at the local dispensary after repeated bouts of diarrhoea.
initiatives: Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) rolled out by Nairobi City County Health Department in maternity facilities
Concern Worldwide maternal, neonatal and child health/nutrition programs in Nairobi's informal settlements
Save the Children urban health and nutrition interventions in Nairobi slums
Nairobi.success_story: Nairobi County, through BFHI and partner-supported urban nutrition programs, has helped push national stunting down from 35.2% (2008-09) to 26% (2014), with continued effort focused on closing the steep slum-vs-formal-settlement gap.

drivers: Highest stunting prevalence in Kenya at ~37% of under-fives, driven by deep rural poverty and food insecurity
Poor dietary intake and sub-optimal infant feeding practices, with low minimum acceptable diet among children 6-23 months
High morbidity from malaria, diarrhoea and respiratory infections that lower immunity and worsen wasting
Low maternal education and limited access to health services in remote coastal villages
Malindi.testimony: Representative composite: Kadzo, a subsistence farmer in rural Kilifi near Malindi, watches her two-year-old daughter grow thinner each dry season as the family's cassava and maize harvest fails. A community health volunteer identified the child as malnourished during a screening and referred her to the nearest dispensary for therapeutic feeding.
initiatives: World Vision Kenya health and nutrition interventions across Kilifi County
Kilifi County Integrated SMART Survey (KNBS-led) coordinating nutrition-specific and -sensitive actors
Kilifi County Department of Health IMAM/CMAM sites and vitamin A supplementation campaigns
Malindi.success_story: Coordinated multi-actor nutrition programming in Kilifi — combining World Vision interventions, IMAM services and the 2023 Integrated SMART Survey — is guiding targeted scaling of infant and young child feeding education and vitamin A/Lipid-based Nutrient Supplement coverage to bring down the county's nation-leading 37% stunting rate.

drivers: Widespread informal settlements (Likoni, Bangladesh, Mnazi Mmoja) with high poverty and overcrowding
Cash-based urban food economy where rising prices push poor households toward low-diversity, calorie-heavy diets
Poor WASH and recurrent diarrhoeal disease in dense slum communities
High unemployment and low maternal education limiting childcare and feeding knowledge
Mombasa.testimony: Representative composite: Mwanaisha, a mother of five in Bangladesh informal settlement, Mombasa, lost her casual portering income during the COVID-19 downturn. With prices of maize and cooking oil climbing, her one-year-old became wasted; she was reached through a community nutrition screening and enrolled in supplementary feeding.
initiatives: WFP food assistance and cash-transfer programs reaching food-insecure Mombasa households (e.g. the 2020 COVID-19 cash transfer of KSh 4,000/month per family)
WHO-AFRO-supported NICK (Nutritional Improvement for Children in Urban Chile and Kenya) intersectoral program in Mombasa's informal settlements
Mombasa County Department of Health maternal and child nutrition clinics
Mombasa.success_story: WFP's COVID-19 cash-transfer program reached vulnerable Mombasa families with KSh 4,000 monthly, covering about half of monthly food and nutrition needs, while the intersectoral NICK model demonstrated that coordinated community-driven action can reduce child malnutrition in urban informal settlements.

drivers: Stunting at ~18% nationally-relevant level but pockets of high malnutrition in urban slums like Obunga
Fishing-community poverty and food insecurity: fish sold for cash rather than household consumption, leaving children with low-diversity diets
High HIV prevalence affecting household food security and childcare capacity
Poor WASH in lakeside informal settlements driving recurrent infections
Kisumu.testimony: Representative composite: Akinyi, a fishmonger in Obunga slum, sells her daily catch at the beach to pay rent, leaving little protein for her own three children. When her youngest, 14 months, became underweight, a community health worker enrolled the family in a Baby-Friendly Community Initiative support group that taught improved complementary feeding.
initiatives: Baby-Friendly Community Initiative (BFCI) led by Kisumu County Government to promote breastfeeding, complementary feeding and maternal nutrition
WiRED International community health worker team conducting malnutrition surveillance and screening
Orange-fleshed sweet potato (OFSP) / vitamin-A biofortification programs in lakeside communities
Kisumu.success_story: Kisumu County's active rollout of the Baby-Friendly Community Initiative — promoting breastfeeding, complementary feeding and WASH — is being scaled countywide as a flagship community-nutrition platform, with improvements in IYCF practices observed in routine health data.

drivers: About 27.6% of under-fives stunted (KDHS 2014, ~75,439 children), with worse rates in informal settlements like Kaptembwo
Urban-rural poverty gap and food insecurity in peri-urban farming households
Sub-optimal infant and young child feeding practices and low maternal nutrition knowledge
Recurrent infections and limited access to quality health services in lower-income areas
Nakuru.testimony: Representative composite: Chebet, a mother of three living in Kaptembwo, Nakuru, struggles to afford a diverse diet on her husband's casual wage. Her two-year-old was flagged as stunted during a clinic visit; she has since joined a county nutrition-support group that introduced low-cost, nutrient-rich recipes.
initiatives: Nutrition International county-level maternal and child nutrition support programs
World Vision Kenya child health and nutrition programming
Nakuru County Government Department of Health nutrition services and GAIN partnerships
Nakuru.success_story: Nakuru County reduced stunting and malnutrition from 28% to 18% over three years through expanded county nutrition services, partner-supported screening and complementary feeding promotion — one of the steepest reductions recorded by a Kenyan county.

drivers: Poverty and food insecurity, particularly in sub-counties like Malava with persistently high stunting and wasting

High disease burden (malaria, diarrhoea) undermining child growth
Large household sizes and low maternal education limiting childcare quality
Kakamega.testimony: Representative composite: Nerima, a smallholder farmer in Malava, Kakamega, feeds her four children mostly maize and occasional vegetables; her youngest, 22 months, was diagnosed as stunted at a child welfare clinic. A community health volunteer helped her start a kitchen garden and incorporate eggs and beans into meals.

Kakamega County Nutrition Scorecard (KHIS-based) for tracking stunting, wasting and underweight
County Government multi-sectoral nutrition programming under the County Nutrition Action Plan
Kakamega.success_story: Kakamega County reduced stunting from 28% (2014) to 12% (2022) and wasting from 11.7% to 2%, attributed to collaborative multi-sectoral efforts by the county government and partners — among Kenya's most pronounced stunting declines.

Market and food-system dynamics that keep nutrient-rich foods out of reach of poor families
Sub-optimal infant feeding and limited maternal nutrition knowledge
Kitale.testimony: Representative composite: Wafula, a maize farmer in Endebess, Trans Nzoia, sells his harvest to pay school fees but cannot afford protein-rich foods for his toddler. During a routine clinic visit the child was found moderately underweight; a health worker referred the family to a community nutrition group supported by AMPATH.

USAID AMPATH Uzima integrated maternal and child health and nutrition services
Kitale.success_story: Trans Nzoia County launched its first-generation County Nutrition Action Plan (2023-2027) with over KSh 14 million committed, anchoring a multi-sectoral approach (AMPATH, USAID and County Health Department) to bring the 21.3% stunting rate below national levels.

Her two-year-old was identified as stunted at an AMPATH-supported clinic; she has since begun nutrition counselling and a small kitchen-garden program.

Eldoret.success_story: Uasin Gishu County developed its first-generation multi-sectoral County Nutrition Action Plan in 2026 to guide nutrition-specific, nutrition-sensitive and enabling interventions — building on AMPATH's long-standing community health platform to curb the 29.4% preschool stunting rate.

The child receives mostly maize porridge and was found underweight at a welfare clinic; Njeri has now joined a county maternal-nutrition support group introducing affordable, diverse meals.

Thika.success_story: Kiambu County, through its County Nutrition Action Plan (CNaP) and partner support, is targeting a 40% reduction in stunting and wasting below 5% by 2025 (aligning with World Health Assembly targets), leveraging UNICEF and Nutrition International support to strengthen maternal and infant nutrition services.

Kilifi.testimony: Representative composite: Kadzo, a subsistence farmer in rural Kilifi near Malindi, watches her two-year-old daughter grow thinner each dry season as the family's cassava and maize harvest fails. A community health volunteer identified the child as malnourished during a screening and referred her to the nearest dispensary for therapeutic feeding.
initiatives: World Vision Kenya health and nutrition interventions across Kilifi County
Kilifi County Integrated SMART Survey (KNBS-led) coordinating nutrition-specific and -sensitive actors
Kilifi County Department of Health IMAM/CMAM sites and vitamin A supplementation campaigns
Kilifi.success_story: Coordinated multi-actor nutrition programming in Kilifi — combining World Vision interventions, IMAM services and the 2023 Integrated SMART Survey — is guiding targeted scaling of infant and young child feeding education and vitamin A/Lipid-based Nutrient Supplement coverage to bring down the county's nation-leading 37% stunting rate.

Market and food-system dynamics that keep nutrient-rich foods out of reach of poor families

During a routine clinic visit the child was found moderately underweight; a health worker referred the family to a community nutrition group supported by AMPATH.
